common_name: Susquehanna Sargent Viburnum (Corky-Barked Heat-Tolerant Sargent Viburnum)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Susquehanna was a U.S. National Arboretum introduction selected for its handsome corky, checkered bark and dense, upright habit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to moist soil in full sun to partial shade, allowing plenty of room for its large, dense, upright-rounded form. Susquehanna was selected at the U.S. National Arboretum for its distinctive corky, deeply furrowed bark that adds winter interest rarely found in the genus, along with maroon-tinged new growth, coarse dark green leaves, and flat white flower clusters in late spring followed by showy red fruit that ages to black. It tolerates heat and heavy clay soil better than many other Viburnum sargentii selections, making it a durable large screening or specimen shrub. Prune only lightly right after flowering to preserve next year's bloom and fruit.

common_name: Cardinal Candy Viburnum (Persistent Red-Fruited Sargent Viburnum)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Cardinal Candy was selected for exceptionally heavy, long-persisting red fruit that birds tend to leave alone until late winter, unlike the quickly stripped fruit of the species.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Cardinal Candy is a compact, rounded Sargent viburnum selection prized above all for its glossy, translucent red berries, which are produced in unusually heavy quantity and hang on the shrub for months into winter rather than being quickly devoured by birds, giving an extended season of bright color against bare branches. Maroon-tinged new growth and creamy-white flat-topped flower clusters in late spring add earlier-season interest. It is a smaller, easier-to-place alternative to straight Viburnum sargentii for foundation plantings and mixed borders where winter fruit display is the main goal. Prune lightly right after flowering, since next year's flowers and fruit form on the current season's wood.

common_name: Mary Milton Doublefile Viburnum (Pink-Flowered Doublefile Viburnum)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Mary Milton is a doublefile viburnum selected for blush-pink lacecap flowers rather than the usual white, and is reported to be less prone to spreading by layering than some doublefile forms.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, siting it where its tiered, horizontally branched habit can be appreciated from above and below. Mary Milton is a doublefile viburnum selected for soft blush-pink lacecap flowers that open in tidy rows along the top of each horizontal branch in late spring, aging to a deeper rose before giving way to red fruit that ripens black. Its layered, wedding-cake branching structure is the signature feature of doublefile viburnums generally, and Mary Milton is reported to hold a somewhat tighter, less rangy habit than older doublefile cultivars. Water regularly during establishment and avoid hot, dry, reflected sites, which stress this species more than most viburnums.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Kilimanjaro was bred for an unusually upright, pyramidal habit that distinguishes it from the wide-spreading form typical of doublefile viburnums.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, giving it room to develop its narrower, more upright profile compared to typical doublefile viburnums. Kilimanjaro still carries the tiered, horizontal branching and rows of white lacecap flowers along each branch in late spring, but its distinctly pyramidal, more vertical growth habit makes it useful as an informal screen or narrow specimen where a wide-spreading doublefile viburnum would not fit. Red fruit ripening to black follows the flowers and draws birds in late summer. Water deeply during dry spells, especially in the first two seasons, since this species performs poorly in hot, dry, or reflected-heat sites.

common_name: Catskill Linden Viburnum (Compact Heavy-Fruiting Linden Viburnum)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Catskill is a U.S. National Arboretum introduction selected for a compact, dense habit and heavy fruit set on a smaller frame than the species.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Catskill is a National Arboretum selection of linden viburnum bred for a noticeably more compact, dense, wider-than-tall habit than the species, which can otherwise reach ten feet or more. Flat clusters of white flowers open in late spring, followed by a heavy set of bright red fruit that persists into winter and draws overwintering birds. Fall color is an attractive mix of yellow, orange, and red, often on the same shrub at once. Its smaller mature size makes it a better fit than straight Viburnum dilatatum for foundation plantings, mixed borders, and smaller gardens. Cross-pollination from an unrelated seedling or cultivar improves fruit set.

common_name: Ogon Golden Linden Viburnum (Chartreuse-Leaved Linden Viburnum)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in partial shade; Ogon is a golden-leaved linden viburnum selection that colors best out of hot afternoon sun, which can scorch its chartreuse foliage.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in partial shade, particularly protection from hot afternoon sun, which can scorch its namesake foliage. Ogon is grown chiefly for its bright chartreuse-to-golden-yellow leaves, a striking foil for the flat white flower clusters that open in late spring and the red fruit that follows in fall. The gold color is most vivid on new growth and in filtered or morning light; full, intense summer sun can bleach or scorch the leaves in hot climates. Otherwise it shares the vigorous, adaptable nature of the species, tolerating a range of soils once established. Site it where its foliage color can be viewed against darker-leaved shrubs or an evergreen backdrop.

common_name: C.A. Hildebrants Arrowwood Viburnum (Compact Native Arrowwood with Fall Color)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; C.A. Hildebrants is a compact selection of native arrowwood viburnum reaching about half the mature size of the wild species.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; C.A. Hildebrants is a compact selection of native arrowwood viburnum, staying at roughly four feet tall and wide compared to the eight- to ten-foot span of the species, making it a better fit for foundation plantings and smaller native gardens. Flat clusters of white flowers open in late spring, followed by blue-black fruit that feeds songbirds, and the glossy dark green summer foliage turns good burgundy-red fall color. Like other arrowwoods it is tough and adaptable, tolerating clay soil, drought, and urban conditions once established, and needs only occasional shaping after bloom.

common_name: Moonglow Arrowwood Viburnum (Glossy-Leaved Native Arrowwood with Domed White Flowers)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Moonglow is a rounded selection of native arrowwood viburnum with glossy foliage and domed clusters of white flowers.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Moonglow is a rounded, evenly proportioned selection of native arrowwood viburnum with unusually glossy, dark green leaves that catch light well against duller-leaved shrubs. Domed clusters of small white flowers open in late spring and are followed by blue-black fruit valued by birds. Its neat rounded habit and reliable, moderate size make it useful as an informal hedge or massed screening planting, and like other arrowwoods it tolerates clay soil, periodic drought, and urban stress once established. Prune to shape immediately after flowering if needed.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Lucidum is a larger-leaved, more vigorous laurustinus selection that is somewhat less cold-hardy than the species.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade, allowing room for a larger, more vigorous shrub than the species type. Lucidum is a classic old laurustinus selection distinguished by larger, glossier, more leathery dark green leaves and generally faster, taller growth, making a substantial evergreen screen or specimen where space allows. Clusters of pink-budded white flowers open from late winter into spring, followed by small dark blue-black fruit. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than typical Viburnum tinus and performs best where winters stay mild; protect from harsh drying winds in its northernmost range. Prune after flowering only as needed to control size, since it can grow larger than many gardeners expect.

common_name: Variegatum Laurustinus Viburnum (Cream and Pink Variegated Laurustinus)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in partial shade; Variegatum is a slower-growing, less vigorous laurustinus selection with cream, yellow, and pink leaf margins that color best out of harsh full sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in partial shade, where its variegated leaf margins hold color best and are less prone to scorch than in harsh full sun. Variegatum is grown for its irregular cream, soft yellow, and blush-pink leaf margins around a dark green center, a striking and unusual look for an evergreen shrub, though it is distinctly slower-growing and less vigorous than green-leaved laurustinus selections. Small clusters of pink-budded white flowers appear from late winter into spring, though flowering is typically lighter than on the species. Because variegated growth is less vigorous, watch for and prune out any reverted all-green shoots, which grow faster and can overtake the variegated portions of the shrub if left unchecked.

common_name: Notcutt European Cranberrybush Viburnum (Large-Flowered Cranberrybush with Red Fall Color)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Notcutt is a European cranberrybush selection bred for larger lacecap flower clusters and strong red fall foliage color.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Notcutt is a selection of European cranberrybush bred for unusually large, showy lacecap flower clusters, with a ring of enlarged sterile white florets surrounding the small fertile center flowers in late spring. Bright red, translucent, currant-like fruit follows in fall and persists into winter if birds leave it alone, and the maple-shaped leaves turn a strong red to burgundy before dropping. It grows into a large, vigorous, arching shrub best used as a specimen, screen, or background planting where its full size can be accommodated. Watch for viburnum leaf beetle, which can heavily defoliate Viburnum opulus selections in parts of its range.

common_name: Aureum Golden European Cranberrybush Viburnum (Golden-Leaved Cranberrybush)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Aureum is a golden-leaved European cranberrybush selection that needs some protection from hot afternoon sun to avoid leaf scorch.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, ideally with protection from intense afternoon sun, which can scorch its namesake foliage color. Aureum is a long-cultivated selection of European cranberrybush grown for bright golden-yellow spring and early-summer foliage that matures toward chartreuse-green as the season progresses, providing season-long color contrast against darker shrubs. It carries the same lacecap white flower clusters and red fruit as the species, though foliage color is the main reason gardeners choose it. Give it morning sun and afternoon shade in hotter climates for the best leaf color without scorching, and watch for viburnum leaf beetle, a significant pest of Viburnum opulus in parts of North America.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Xanthocarpum is a long-cultivated European cranberrybush selection grown for translucent yellow rather than red fruit.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Xanthocarpum is a classic, long-grown selection of European cranberrybush distinguished from the species chiefly by its fruit, which ripens to a translucent amber-yellow rather than the typical bright red, and tends to hang on the shrub longer since birds often pass over yellow fruit in favor of red. Lacecap white flower clusters open in late spring, and the maple-like leaves color in shades of yellow and red-purple in fall. It grows into a large, arching shrub best suited to a background border, screen, or specimen planting with room to spread. Watch for viburnum leaf beetle, which can be a serious defoliating pest of Viburnum opulus selections.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

common_name: Chenaultii Burkwood Viburnum (Looser Fragrant Burkwood Viburnum Clone)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Chenaultii is a looser, more graceful, and reportedly hardier clone of Burkwood viburnum than the original Burkwood and Skipwith selection.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Chenaultii is an early clone of Burkwood viburnum, a hybrid of Viburnum carlesii and V. utile, valued for the same intensely fragrant, pink-budded white flower clusters that open in mid-spring before or with the emerging leaves. Compared to the original Burkwood and Skipwith introduction, Chenaultii tends to grow looser and more graceful rather than densely upright, with semi-evergreen foliage in milder climates that may turn burgundy in fall where it drops. Site it near a path, door, or window where its spring fragrance can be enjoyed up close. Prune lightly right after flowering to maintain shape without sacrificing next year's bloom.
sources: Dirr's Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

common_name: Angustifolium Narrow-Leaf Possumhaw Viburnum (Compact Smooth Witherod with Crimson Fall Color)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Angustifolium is a smaller, narrow-leaved selection of native smooth witherod with especially vivid wine-burgundy to crimson fall color.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Angustifolium is a compact selection of native smooth witherod distinguished by narrower green leaves than the species and exceptionally vivid fall color, turning shades of wine-burgundy to crimson before dropping. Flat white flower clusters open in early summer, followed by clusters of pink, blue, and purple fruit that ripen unevenly and often show several colors on the same cluster at once. Its smaller stature compared to the species fits rain gardens, pond margins, and low, damp spots in the landscape where its cousins Winterthur and Brandywine might grow too large. It tolerates both wet, poorly drained soil and average garden conditions once established.
